analysis.one_liner: Bans new oil, gas, mining, and geothermal leases around Chaco Culture park and kills dormant leases.
analysis.headline: Introduced in April 2025, the bill has received no hearing or vote in the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would withdraw federal land in a buffer zone around Chaco Culture National Historical Park — a UNESCO World Heritage site in New Mexico — from all new mineral leasing, mining, and geothermal development. It would automatically terminate oil and gas leases in the zone that have never produced. It explicitly leaves tribal mineral rights on tribal trust and allotment land untouched, and allows the Secretary of the Interior to convey federal land in the zone to Indian tribes.
analysis.who_benefits: Pueblo tribes, the Navajo Nation, and the Hopi Tribe, whose members use the Greater Chaco landscape for ceremony and who live alongside existing natural gas development, plus park visitors and neighboring communities concerned about air, water, and night-sky impacts from expanded drilling under the Mancos/Gallup shale play.

how_it_helps.text: It withdraws the buffer-zone federal land from all forms of mineral leasing, mining entry, and geothermal leasing, subject to valid existing rights.
It terminates oil and gas leases in the zone that never began drilling and never produced in paying quantities, and bars the Secretary from extending them.

The bill's findings state that renewed oil exploration in the Mancos/Gallup shale play threatens cultural resources, the park's visitor experience, and the health and safety of nearby tribal communities.
It preserves tribal and Navajo allottee mineral rights and allows water, power, and road improvements and conveyance of federal land to tribes.

analysis.who_pays: Companies holding dormant federal oil and gas leases inside the buffer zone, which lose those leases by operation of law, and any mining or geothermal interests that hoped to claim federal land in the zone. New Mexico and counties also forgo future federal mineral revenue-sharing from that acreage, though existing producing operations and tribal mineral rights continue.
analysis.who_pays_short: Holders of dormant oil and gas leases

drawbacks.text: Federal mineral royalties are shared with states and counties, so withdrawing the acreage permanently removes a potential revenue stream that supports local governments in northwest New Mexico.
Companies that paid for nonproducing federal leases inside the zone have those leases terminated by law rather than letting them lapse on their own schedule.

A permanent statutory withdrawal forecloses any future development regardless of technology or circumstance, while the alternative in place — a 2023 federal withdrawal — can be revisited or modified by a later administration.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill trades a bounded, permanent loss of federal mineral development on land immediately surrounding a World Heritage site for protection of cultural resources and the communities that live with drilling impacts. The economic cost is limited to dormant leases and future leasing on federal acreage in the buffer, since producing wells and tribal mineral rights are preserved; the main honest criticism is that permanence removes the flexibility a future administration might want.

outcome.mechanism: The bill went to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee when it was introduced in April 2025 and has had no hearing, markup, or vote since.

narrative.text: Sen. Ben Ray Luján introduced the bill with Sen. Martin Heinrich on April 10, 2025; it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources.
No further action is listed in the bill's history — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action.

The bill would enact into permanent law a mineral withdrawal around Chaco Culture National Historical Park, building on a withdrawal map the Bureau of Land Management prepared in 2022 for a proposed federal withdrawal.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies holding dormant federal leases in the buffer zone keep those leases alive for now, and the possibility of renewed leasing after the current federal withdrawal ends in 2033 remains open because no permanent statutory protection has been enacted.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Holders of dormant oil and gas leases

for.name: Sen. Ben Ray Luján
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Chaco Cultural Heritage Area Protection Act of 2025.

for.name: Sen. Martin Heinrich
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's sole cosponsor at introduction.

for.name: Pueblo, Navajo, and Hopi communities in the Greater Chaco region
for.role: Tribes and local residents living near existing natural gas development
for.what_they_did: Tribal communities have publicly pressed for federal protection of the Greater Chaco landscape from expanded oil and gas development across multiple administrations.

against.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee (Chair Mike Lee)
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill in the months since it was referred on April 10, 2025.

sides.party_line_note: Only two Democratic senators from New Mexico are attached to the bill; no committee or floor votes exist, so the partisan shape is not yet visible.

industries.industry: Oil and gas operators (Mancos/Gallup shale, San Juan Basin)
industries.note: The bill terminates nonproducing federal leases in the buffer zone and bars all future federal leasing there. Its interest in expanding drilling around the park runs against the communities and tribes living with the wellfield's health and air-quality impacts.
Federal land in the zone is withdrawn from mining entry and geothermal leasing, foreclosing any future claims or leases there.

industries.industry: New Mexico state and San Juan County governments
industries.note: They forgo future federal mineral royalty sharing on the withdrawn acreage, but residents of the county are among those protected from expanded drilling near the park.

analysis.trajectory: With a Republican committee chair and no hearing as of now, the bill is very unlikely to advance this Congress; similar Chaco buffer bills in prior Congresses never reached a floor vote. Interim protection exists through a 2023 federal mineral withdrawal around the park that runs for 20 years, so the practical question — and the case for making protection permanent in law — returns as that withdrawal approaches its end.
